https://www.lancashiretelegraph.co.uk/ne.text: People Lancaster-born woman died after spinal injury from fall, inquest hears By James Richings News and Sports Reporter Share 0 Comments (Image: NQ) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A Lancaster -born woman who "loved books, animals and people" died after suffering a spinal injury following a fall at her home, an inquest heard. Beaconsfield Coroner's Court heard how Wanda Jadwiga Van-Der-Zyden, known to family and friends as Lou, was found dead at her home in High Wycombe on April 18 this year, at the age of 72. Assistant Coroner Gemma Brannigan, who conducted the inquest on July 22, recorded a conclusion of accidental death. The hearing was attended by Ms Van-Der-Zyden's sister Barbra, daughter Zara, and Zara’s partner, David. A pen portrait written by Zara was read out by the coroner, describing her mother as a caring and compassionate woman. Born in Lancaster, she was of Polish heritage and grew up with three siblings. The court heard how the 72-year-old had fond memories of family life and was particularly proud of returning to education as a mature student in her 40s. She later worked as a librarian at Buckinghamshire New University, where she enjoyed helping students and supporting them in their studies. However, several serious health conditions, including brain surgery, a stroke and breast cancer, meant she retired on ill-health grounds. Zara described her mother as a devoted animal lover who cared deeply about the natural world. A pescatarian, she supported charitable causes and adored her pets, including an energetic kitten which now lives with her daughter. "She loved books, animals, people, was always caring and had a good heart," Zara said. The inquest heard the family became concerned after messages sent to Ms Van-Der-Zyden went unanswered, with the last known contact taking place on April 16, two days before she was found. After emergency services were called, South Central Ambulance Service and Thames Valley Police attended the property and discovered the 72-year-old near the bottom of the staircase. Her death was formally confirmed at 9.39pm on April 18. Evidence heard during the inquest suggested she may have been heading upstairs when she fell, although the precise circumstances could not be determined. Consultant pathologist Dr Sukhvinder Ghataura, who gave evidence remotely, said Ms Van-Der-Zyden had suffered a fracture-dislocation at the top of her spine, close to the brain stem. He also found evidence of significant heart disease, including an enlarged heart and narrowed coronary arteries. Dr Ghataura said it was not possible to determine whether a cardiac event had caused the fall or whether the fall occurred first and led to fatal complications. It was concluded that both factors likely contributed to her death. Recording her conclusion, the coroner accepted the medical evidence and found that Ms Van-Der-Zyden died from traumatic spine fracture dislocation with heart disease. She said it was unclear exactly how the fall occurred and that she could not determine whether a cardiac event had preceded it, but was satisfied that Ms Van-Der-Zyden had suffered a fall at home. The inquest, which lasted roughly an hour, ended with the coroner offering her condolences to the family and reminding them to "remember the fond memories" they shared with Ms Van-Der-Zyden. Photograph: Juan Algar/Getty Images Energy Australia’s dependence on gas generation during evening energy peak falls by almost 70% Batteries now meet almost half of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during hours of highest demand Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Petra Stock Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australia’s dependence on gas for power during the evening, when the grid is under the most pressure, has fallen by almost nearly 70% over the past year as batteries surged in, replacing the fossil fuel . Gas generation during the busy early evening, between 5pm and 8pm, fell by 67% in the year to August, as large-scale batteries continued to come online and half a million home batteries were installed under the government’s subsidy program, analysis by consultancy EnergyEdge found. The company’s managing director, Josh Stabler, said batteries big and small recorded their highest peak output on record, off the back of rapid uptake. “The rate of installation of batteries in Australia is the fastest uptake of any electricity asset ever – faster than solar, faster than wind,” he said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email According to the EnergyEdge report: “batteries have taken the evening peak, and they’re not giving it back”. Batteries met 49% of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during the evening in August 2026, up from 0.4% in 2020. In contrast, gas fell from 65.9% to 20.6% over the same period. Wholesale electricity prices fell in response – a win for households – but potentially a problem for future investment in new dispatchable power. Recent quarterly data (April to June) from the Australian Energy Market Operator highlighted a similar pattern, with gas generation recording its lowest Q2 on average in more than two decades. Gas power declined in all regions, the AEMO said, with the fall “most evident” during the evening peak. The Grattan Institute’s energy and climate change program director, Alison Reeve, said utility scale batteries were increasingly mopping up surplus renewable energy in the middle of the day and displacing the role of gas during the peak. What you actually end up doing is flattening out the load curve over the day,” she said, and that reduced volatility in the system. In the longer term, less gas and lower volatility should be good for prices, she said. Although the declining demand and added uncertainty could make gas more expensive and less profitable at those times when it was needed – in those few dark, still and cold weeks in winter. “That’s kind of the challenge that is coming for gas,” she said. “We know that gas generators are going to be important, because they’re going to be the backup when you get those two weeks in winter where solar, wind and batteries can’t carry you through.” AEMO’s 20-year roadmap , the Integrated System Plan, anticipated gas would play “a more strategic, back-up role, with flexible generators that can also provide system security service” in future. “This is more likely to be in winter, especially in the southern states, when shorter days reduce solar output, and when more electricity is needed for longer and colder nights. “Gas is going through a transition and its whole role is going to change,” Reeve said, a shift that would affect the amount of gas needed, the number of generators and the running costs. “The sooner that we actually grasp that the future for gas generators is going to look nothing like the past, the better we will be at managing that whole process and making sure it doesn’t end up costing people a lot of money.” Explore more on these topics Energy Energy storage Fossil fuels Gas news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
